title: Chunking 101: windows, overlap, the tradeoff
summary: The real reason to chunk is not context limits, it is that a long document's vector dilutes every term by about 1/sqrt(k). Overlap patches the boundary problem at a storage cost you can compute, and the famous 512 token default is folklore from BERT's architecture.
html:
You have been assuming chunks exist since Day 2. Today you decide how to make them, and this is the first decision in the course that is genuinely irreversible in practice. Change your scorer and you rerun a query. Change your chunking and you re-embed the entire corpus and every measurement you took before is void.

Three reasons to chunk, and only one that still matters

The reason usually given is that documents do not fit in the context window. That was the binding constraint in 2022. It is much weaker now, since a 1M token window holds something like a 2000 page corpus, and on Day 91 you will look at when retrieval can be skipped entirely for small corpora.

The second reason is cost. You pay per input token on every query, forever. Sending a whole document to answer one question is a recurring bill for text nobody read.

The third reason is the real one, and it survives any context window: precision of the embedding itself. One vector per document means one vector describing everything that document is about, and that is a much worse representation than it sounds.

Dilution, with numbers

Here is the mechanism, using the normalisation you built yesterday.

Take a document with k distinct terms of roughly comparable weight. After L2 normalisation the vector has unit length, so those k components share a total squared length of 1. Each individual component lands around 1/sqrt(k).

k =   70 distinct terms  ->  each term's weight ~ 0.120
k =  400 distinct terms  ->  each term's weight ~ 0.050
k = 2000 distinct terms  ->  each term's weight ~ 0.022

A 100 word chunk has maybe 70 distinct terms. A 10,000 word document has maybe 2000. The same term, mentioned the same number of times, carries about 5.3 times less weight in the long document purely because it is competing with more vocabulary for a fixed unit of length.

So a document containing one excellent paragraph about queen bees, surrounded by nine thousand words about hive economics, has a vector that points mostly at hive economics. Query for queens and it loses to a short document that is entirely about them, even though your paragraph is the better answer. The information is in your index and is unreachable.

That is the argument for chunking, and notice it has nothing to do with context windows.

Fixed-size windows

The baseline algorithm, and the one worth starting with:

size   = words per chunk
overlap = words repeated from the previous chunk
stride = size - overlap          how far the window advances

chunks = ceil( (total_words - overlap) / stride )

Two parameters, and the second one exists to patch a problem the first one creates.

The boundary problem

A fixed window cuts at word 512 regardless of what is there. If the sentence "the queen lays up to 1000 eggs per day" straddles that boundary, one chunk ends with "the queen lays up to" and the next starts with "1000 eggs per day". Neither chunk answers the question. The fact is in your corpus, correctly ingested, and permanently unfindable.

Overlap is the mitigation. Repeat the tail of each chunk at the head of the next, and any span shorter than the overlap is guaranteed to appear intact somewhere. It costs storage:

sizeoverlapstridechunks per 10k wordsstorage
5120512201.02x
51264448231.18x
512128384261.33x
512256256392.00x

The multiplier is roughly size / stride, and it applies to your vector storage, your index build time, and your index memory. Fifty percent overlap doubles all three. For a corpus where that is 400 GB of vectors rather than 200 GB (Day 27 covers what that costs), the decision is a capacity plan, not a preference.

Ten to twenty percent overlap is the usual compromise. Be clear that it is a compromise and not a fix:

  • It only protects spans shorter than the overlap. An answer needing three paragraphs of context is still split, and no overlap setting rescues it.
  • It creates near-duplicate chunks, so your top 5 can contain the same text twice and you have wasted a retrieval slot. Day 38 deals with deduplication in the cascade.
  • It inflates document frequency for terms in overlap regions, which skews the IDF you built on Day 4. The effect is small, but it is real, and it is the kind of thing that makes two implementations disagree.

What size, honestly

You will read that 512 tokens is the right chunk size. That number is folklore with a traceable origin: it is BERT's maximum sequence length, an architectural limit from 2018, not a finding about retrieval quality. Plenty of current embedding models accept 8192 tokens and the number persists anyway.

What actually decides it is the shape of answers in your corpus. Ask what a correct answer physically looks like in your documents. If it is a single sentence from a spec, small chunks win, because precision is everything and context is already in the surrounding text. If it is a six step procedure that only makes sense whole, cutting it at 200 words guarantees you retrieve step four without steps one to three.

Common practice sits between 200 and 800 words. Anyone who gives you a single number without asking about your corpus is guessing. The honest answer is that you measure it, and you cannot measure it until you have the harness from Day 57, which is exactly why that phase exists.

One thing that is not a judgement call: never let a fixed splitter cut a table in half. A half table is garbage for both embedding and generation. Structure-aware splitting on Day 40 handles this properly.

Everything today was counted in words because words are easy to reason about. Models do not charge by the word, and the unit they do charge by does not map cleanly onto words at all. Tomorrow is tokens: what they are, and what they cost.
exercise:
1. Measure dilution on your own text. Take a long document, 2000 words or more. Build a TF-IDF vector for the whole thing as one unit, then chunk it at 150 words and build vectors for each chunk. Pick a term that appears in exactly one paragraph and compare its normalized weight in the whole document vector against its weight in the chunk that contains it. Ratio should be several times. That ratio is the reason you chunk.

2. Compute your storage bill. For a corpus size you actually care about, work out chunk count and storage multiplier at 0, 10, and 50 percent overlap using the formulas above. If you were storing 1024-dimension float32 vectors, how many GB is each option? You will need this number again on Day 27.

3. Break a boundary on purpose. Chunk a document with zero overlap, then find a fact that got cut across the seam. Query for it with your Day 5 scorer and watch it fail to surface. Re-chunk with 20 percent overlap and watch it come back. Ten minutes, and it makes the tradeoff concrete rather than theoretical.
